items.correctExplanation: Right — vaccines stage harmless rehearsals so memory cells answer encores fast. Training, never shielding, protects.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — rehearsals, not shields. Shots teach immune memory; the body performs on opening night.
items.lessonContent:
Vaccines rehearse immune orchestras safely.
Memory cells recall encores rapidly.
Rehearsals beat opening-night surprises.
Share this: call boosters encore practice.
items.question: How do vaccines protect against future infection?
items.title: The Immune Rehearsal

items.correctExplanation: Correct — immune memory wanes over years; boosters refresh the lesson. Recall needs rehearsal.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, memory cells fade. Boosters re-teach guards whose textbooks yellowed.
items.lessonContent:
Immune memory fades like all memories.
Boosters refresh fading textbooks.
Schedules match waning curves.
Share this: check one booster due date.
items.question: Why do some vaccines need boosters?
items.title: The Fading Lesson

items.correctExplanation: Yes — immune majorities break every chain the virus tries. Stalled spread shelters the vulnerable few.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Starving transmission chains. High coverage denies pathogens their next hosts.
items.lessonContent:
Herd immunity starves pathogens of hosts.
Thresholds vary with contagiousness.
Majorities shield minorities medically.
Share this: explain thresholds with wildfire gaps.
items.question: How does herd immunity protect the unvaccinated?
items.title: The Broken Chain

items.correctExplanation: Right — mRNA delivers temporary protein recipes; cells recycle them within days. Messages, never edits, immunize.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — instruction slips, not alterations. The slips degrade; DNA archives stay untouched.
items.lessonContent:
mRNA vaccines message, never modify.
Cells recycle instructions within days.
Recipes cook proteins, then vanish.
Share this: retire the DNA-alteration myth.
items.question: Do mRNA vaccines alter human DNA?
items.title: The Temporary Note

items.correctExplanation: Correct — antibodies tag invaders while killer T-cells execute infected cells. Tag-teams clear infections.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, tags plus assassins. B-cells label; T-cells destroy the labeled.
items.lessonContent:
Antibodies tag; T-cells terminate.
Humoral and cellular arms cooperate.
Tests measure tags, not always troops.
Share this: name both arms of defense.
items.question: What are the respective jobs of antibodies and killer T-cells?
items.title: The Tag Team

items.correctExplanation: Yes — innate guards attack everything instantly; adaptive forces study then remember. Speed first, precision second.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Fast generalists, slow specialists. Skin and inflammation hold the line while lymphocytes learn.
items.lessonContent:
Innate immunity reacts instantly and generally.
Adaptive immunity learns slowly, remembers forever.
Layers cooperate across timescales.
Share this: feel innate heat in one paper cut.
items.question: How do innate and adaptive immunity differ?
items.title: The Two Armies

items.correctExplanation: Right — raised heat hobbles many pathogens while mobilizing defenses. Fever is thermostat warfare.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — cooking germs slowly. Immune command raises set-points deliberately.
items.lessonContent:
Fevers weaponize temperature against germs.
Set-points rise by immune orders.
Mild fevers merit respect and rest.
Share this: rest one mild fever out.
items.question: Why does the immune system cause fever?
items.title: The Inner Furnace

items.correctExplanation: Correct — vessels dilate to flood the site with troops and supplies. Swelling is logistics, not damage.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, battlefield swelling. Redness and heat mark supply lines, not defeat.
items.lessonContent:
Inflammation delivers troops through widened roads.
Swelling is logistics made visible.
Chronic alarms, not acute ones, harm.
Share this: ice one sprain understandingly.
items.question: What purpose does inflammation serve?
items.title: The Red Flood

items.correctExplanation: Yes — harmless pollen trips defenses built for parasites. Allergies are security overreactions.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Misfired alarms. IgE antibodies panic at dust that never threatened.
items.lessonContent:
Allergies misfire parasite alarms at pollen.
Hygiene shifts may tune sensitivity.
Desensitization retrains the guards.
Share this: forgive one sneezy overreaction.
items.question: What causes allergies to harmless pollen?
items.title: The False Alarm

items.correctExplanation: Right — tolerance training fails and guards attack the host. Autoimmunity is civil war.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — self-recognition failure. Thymus schooling misfires; own tissues read as foreign.
items.lessonContent:
Tolerance training usually prevents civil war.
Thymus schools guards on self-portraits.
Failures ignite autoimmune battles.
Share this: respect the thymus's quiet schooling.
items.question: What goes wrong in autoimmune disease?
items.title: The Friendly Fire

items.correctExplanation: Correct — measles deletes immune memories, leaving amnesia toward past foes. Vaccination guards the guards.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, memory-wiping infection. Survivors must relearn defeated diseases.
items.lessonContent:
Measles wipes immune hard drives alarmingly.
Amnesia invites old foes back freely.
Shots protect memories themselves.
Share this: vaccinate to keep immune memories.
items.question: Why do measles survivors catch old illnesses again?
items.title: The Forgotten Foes

items.correctExplanation: Yes — flu mutates its coat yearly, outrunning last year's memory. Drift demands annual rehearsals.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Shape-shifting surface. Antigenic drift redesigns the viral uniform each season.
items.lessonContent:
Flu redesigns its coat annually.
Drift outruns static immune memories.
Shots update the wanted posters.
Share this: get this season's poster update.
items.question: Why is last year's flu shot outdated?
items.title: The New Disguise

items.correctExplanation: Right — 'colds' are hundreds of viruses wearing similar sniffles. No single shot covers the crowd.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — hundred-plus disguises. Rhinovirus legions plus cousins defy one cure.
items.lessonContent:
Colds are crowds, never single culprits.
Serotype legions outnumber shots feasible.
Hygiene beats silver bullets here.
Share this: wash hands against the legion.
items.question: Why is there no cure for the common cold?
items.title: The Crowded Sniffle

items.correctExplanation: Correct — maternal antibodies patrol newborns for months. Mothers lend patrols before babies build their own.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, borrowed starter immunity. Placenta and milk transfer ready-made guards.
items.lessonContent:
Mothers lend immune patrols to newborns.
Borrowed antibodies bridge vulnerable months.
Vaccines later build owned armies.
Share this: honor milk's quiet armory.
items.question: How are newborns protected before their own immunity builds?
items.title: The Lent Shield

items.correctExplanation: Yes — chickenpox virus sleeps in nerves for decades, then erupts as shingles. Old foes nap, never leave.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Dormant virus reawakens. Childhood pox wires adult shingles' fuse.
items.lessonContent:
Chickenpox viruses hibernate in nerve roots.
Aging immunity loosens the leash.
Shingles shots reinforce old guards.
Share this: ask elders about shingles shots.
items.question: Why can chickenpox return as shingles decades later?
items.title: The Sleeping Foe

items.correctExplanation: Right — pus is mostly dead neutrophils plus debris. Battlefields bury their own.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — fallen soldier pile. White cells die killing; pus archives the war.
items.lessonContent:
Pus archives immune battlefields faithfully.
Neutrophils die killing in droves.
Drainage clears the graveyard helpfully.
Share this: respect one healing scab's work.
items.question: What is pus mostly made of?
items.title: The White Graveyard

items.correctExplanation: Correct — nodes are headquarters where scouts brief lymphocytes. Swelling means war councils in session.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, command-post swelling. Glands enlarge as defenders multiply inside.
items.lessonContent:
Lymph nodes host immune war councils.
Scouts brief lymphocytes within swollen walls.
Tender glands signal active defense.
Share this: feel one gland mid-cold knowingly.
items.question: Why do glands swell during infections?
items.title: The Busy Headquarters

items.correctExplanation: Yes — soap molecules pry apart viral lipid envelopes. Twenty seconds dissolves armor.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Envelope-dissolving soap. Suds split fatty coats; water rinses the wreckage.
items.lessonContent:
Soap dissolves viral envelopes chemically.
Twenty seconds completes the demolition.
Friction plus chemistry beats rinsing.
Share this: sing through one full wash.
items.question: How does soap destroy viruses?
items.title: The Sudsy Demolition

items.correctExplanation: Right — antibiotics sabotage bacterial machinery viruses lack. Prescribing them for flu wastes arsenals and breeds resistance.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — bacteria-only weapons. Wall-builders and protein-forges exist solely in bacteria.
items.lessonContent:
Antibiotics target bacterial machinery exclusively.
Viruses offer no walls to wreck.
Misuse breeds resistant survivors.
Share this: refuse antibiotics for colds.
items.question: Why can't antibiotics cure viral infections?
items.title: The Wrong Arsenal

items.correctExplanation: Correct — trillions of microbes train immunity and crowd out invaders. Gardens, not deserts, defend guts.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, inner ecosystem balance. Diverse flora outcompetes pathogens for niches.
items.lessonContent:
Microbiomes train immune tolerance daily.
Diversity crowds out invading pathogens.
Antibiotics clear-cut the garden.
Share this: feed your flora fiber today.
items.question: How do gut microbes protect health?
items.title: The Inner Garden

items.correctExplanation: Yes — transplants carrying foreign MHC tags trigger rejection. Guards read molecular passports ruthlessly.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Identity-tag mismatch. Mismatched self-markers convict donor organs.
items.lessonContent:
MHC tags passport every cell's identity.
Transplants must match molecular papers.
Suppression drugs bribe the border guards.
Share this: register as an organ donor.
items.question: Why do transplanted organs get rejected?
items.title: The Foreign Passport

items.correctExplanation: Right — blood plasma carries antibodies against foreign ABO antigens. Mismatched transfusions trigger instant battle.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — pre-made plasma weapons. Type O lacks antigens; AB lacks antibodies — the compatibility grid follows.
items.lessonContent:
ABO antibodies patrol plasma pre-made.
Antigens invite attack when mismatched.
Typing prevents transfusion wars.
Share this: learn your own blood type.
items.question: Why must blood types match for transfusion?
items.title: The Typed River

items.correctExplanation: Correct — horses dosed with venom brew antibodies harvested as antivenom. Equine factories bottle cures.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, horse-trained serum. Immunized horses donate antibody-rich plasma for victims.
items.lessonContent:
Horses manufacture antivenom at scale.
Graduated venom doses train equine blood.
Serum harvests save snakebite victims.
Share this: thank one serum horse silently.
items.question: How is snake antivenom produced?
items.title: The Equine Factory

items.correctExplanation: Yes — CCR5 mutations remove HIV's favorite doorway. Missing handles bar entry genetically.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Locked cellular door. Delta-32 carriers lack the co-receptor HIV grasps.
items.lessonContent:
CCR5 mutations bar HIV's entry door.
Genetic resistance inspires drug designs.
Berlin patients proved the principle.
Share this: marvel at one protective mutation.
items.question: Why are some people naturally resistant to HIV?
items.title: The Missing Handle

items.correctExplanation: Right — milkmaids' cowpox exposure blocked smallpox. Related germs cross-train guards effectively.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — cowpox cross-training. Jenner weaponized the dairymaid observation into vaccination.
items.lessonContent:
Cowpox cross-trained guards against smallpox.
Jenner tested folklore scientifically.
Observation plus experiment births vaccines.
Share this: retell Jenner's milkmaid insight.
items.question: How did Jenner's first vaccine work?
items.title: The Milkmaid Clue
